collins.hedgehog: Become best in the world at building global brands of everyday consumer necessities that require sophisticated manufacturing technology (shaving systems first, later toothbrushes and similar products). The economics run on high-margin repeat purchases, so profit per customer is the denominator. The passion is a love of the technology of shaving and of world-class products.
hedgehog_key_points: high-margin repeat purchase; profit per customer
collins.stop_doing: Stop the scattered diversification of the previous era (watches, calculators, fire extinguishers, Welcome Wagon, Hyponex and similar). Refuse to bet the shaving business on cheap, low-margin disposables; invest instead in premium shaving systems (which led to Sensor).
collins.leader_type: Level 5 (Colman Mockler: reserved, gracious, a finance insider; ferociously persistent. He fought off takeover attempts (Perelman 1986, Coniston 1988) to protect long-term investment in Sensor, and died in 1991 soon after Sensor's success).
brutal_facts: blades produce about 71% of pretax profit, while lighters and pens are weak
Bic is attacking on price across pens, lighters and razors

later_history: Bought Oral-B in 1984 for $188.5M. Beat back Perelman's $4.1B approach (1986) and Coniston's proxy fight (1988); Berkshire Hathaway invested $600M in 1989. Sensor (1989-90) was a major success, followed by Mach3 (1998). Collins reports cumulative returns about 7.39x the market for 1980-1995. Bought Duracell in 1996 for $7.1B. Merged into Procter & Gamble on 1 October 2005.
notes: Track A matched pair with A10 (Warner-Lambert). Mockler became CEO in 1975, five years before Collins's 1980 transition date. The disposables decision is confirmed by a secondary summary of Collins (Compound Learning); the hedgehog wording is paraphrased from memory of Ch. 5. Warner-Lambert owned Schick, so the two companies were direct rivals in shaving.
